fields.description:
Each tool shares through a local bare repository in the scratch root, as its docs prescribe: bead publishes every write; bd runs `bd dolt push` to refs/dolt/data; br exports, commits .beads/ and pushes. Time a session of agent loops until a second clone sees the work, and record how much the remote grew.

Start-up: the first ready in a new worktree (bead's worktrees share its store, bd's share the main database, br's has no database yet) and in a fresh clone joining the tracker (bead init; bd joining from refs/dolt/data; br importing the clone's JSONL).
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- summary.md gains, per size, the shared session, both start-ups and the remote's growth per 1,000 writes.
- The second clone's answers pass the answer check against the first's.
fields.title: Comparison harness: shared sessions, start-up in a new worktree or clone, remote growth

fields.description:
Two, four and eight agents at once, each tool set up as its docs recommend for several agents: bead in a worktree each; br as that many processes in one checkout; bd in worktrees on its embedded database and, as a variant, in server mode, which needs a dolt binary, pinned and verified like the others. Measure throughput, p50 and p95 per loop and errors by kind (lock timeouts, refusals); afterwards count writes lost and issues two agents both believed they held.

Optionally, a manually triggered CI workflow that runs the two smaller sizes with the pinned tools and uploads summary.md. GitHub's runners are noisy: its figures show trends, not precise ratios.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- summary.md gains the concurrency table for two, four and eight agents, per tool.
- Each run's check counts lost writes and issues claimed twice.
fields.title: Comparison harness: concurrent agents, bd's server mode, an optional CI job

data.text: Progress (br-edges): 5c079d3 pins what every issue's edges answer on 9cbd60a's code (projection/tests/edges.rs: edges, tags and metadata in order, readiness, blockers, parents, children, dependents, cycles, ready, details, export; digests per seed of every batch of the plain, flawed, awaiting and delivery-order histories; three bead-built journals in full, one new with seven kinds, imported metadata, a merged cycle, concurrent and re-added edges). d073dea extends the differential generator (projection/tests/edges/drawn.rs) with targets naming no issue, new kinds, imports with metadata, concurrent and re-added edges, edges to renamed copies, and read_back compares each edge's metadata. Next: the typed representation. Design: Edge { to: Target (Id(EventId) when the text is an id's spelling, else Text), kind: Arc<str> interned via the codec's name table }; the state part keeps each edge's addition ids, the metadata goes in a section appended to the issue's text record; an op that changes an issue's edges (dep_add, dep_remove, a create binding awaited entries in another issue) needs its texts read in, or extension declines.

Shared code beyond the texts mechanism (br-edges, for the orchestrator to relay to br-ownership): with each edge addition's metadata in the issue's texts, an edge change needs the issue's texts read in. dep_add and dep_remove are about their issue, which stores already read in; but a create whose key an import of another issue waits for makes an edge in that other issue (replay::apply::create::bind), which no record names. I am adding Projection::about(&records) in beadroll-core: the issues records name, plus those waiting by an imported dependency for a key a create among them brings. The store's projection::about (beadroll-store/src/projection.rs, current) and the transaction's (beadroll-sync/src/tx.rs, Emitter::state) call it instead of reading each record's issue themselves; Projection::extend declines when such an issue's texts are not in, as it does for long fields. No other change to how texts are read or written. br-ownership: if your history moves need a wider 'about', add to that function rather than the two callers. Orchestrator: tx.rs's change is in Emitter::state only, not finish/publish_soon.

Step 1 committed (4a119c0, green on 9cbd60a's code): projection::tests::owned pins every issue's claim, generation, claim_history, provisional, lost, stale, detail and export, line by line on three bead-built journals (golden, fleet, a two-machine ownership store with a planted lost claim) and by digest on every differential/delivery-order history plus an ownership-heavy world of its own; commands::ownership pins the end-to-end transcript (every write's answer; show/export/claims/prime/list/ready/blocked human and --json on two machines). Readers found: no command prints claim_history; only commands::ended_by (close/delete/update decisions, on states whose texts are not read in: plan.left subtrees, every target) reads its last entry's ended_by and how; transition::superseded reads stale ends from view_outline after a publish; show/claim/takeover/update details print lost_claims and stale (texts read in by view_of). Replay's claim code only appends. Plan: Stored keeps the last ended claim's (ended_by, how) unread; superseded reads in the texts of the issues its close named; extend's texts_in counts claim/release/close/reopen/delete as touching texts (declines when There), and replay marks texts changed (Read->Here) only when it appends to the history.

data.text: Implemented on branch no-remote-write-keeps-transaction: beadroll_sync::destination chooses where a write goes (None when --offline, no remote, or a remote with no URL; the endpoint or the error choosing it otherwise) and publish_soon_at publishes to it; publish_soon is the two together. cli::finish chooses the destination before ended_with and frees the transaction first only for Some(Ok(_)), so a write on a tracker with no remote keeps it to the end of the process, and a remote that cannot be chosen keeps it and is reported as before. data.text:
Design (br-copy, roll-lqjj.44 and .45; steps 4 and 5 of roll-lqjj.36, X17): a write-back that copies the bytes of what the write did not touch, then one that appends what changed. Nothing implemented yet; waiting for go.

HOW IT WAS MEASURED. fd5ae9b, release, on the shared 64-core machine (load 3-4 from other agents), so absolute figures are inflated; only runs made together are compared. In process: a scratch probe, not committed: a copy of fd5ae9b (git archive) whose Projection::encode_with is copied into an encode_phases that times each phase and records each issue's and each event record's offset (the issues loop of write_state split from the rest, write_events split into the records and the machines), driven from timing --decode's history (PHASES=1 cargo xtask timing --decode N [--ownership]), best of 5 per phase; assembling, summing and writing timed on the bytes encode gave, as file::bytes and write_cache_parts do them (a Vec of header + parts, sum() of each part, write + rename in target/, not fsynced). End to end: the committed cargo xtask timing --read N and --sync N, three runs each, best kept. Heap: cargo xtask bead (a wrapper as BEAD_UNDER_TEST) on the store timing --read builds. If the step lands I will put the phase split into timing --decode for the PR (copied vs fresh encode), so that its figures come from a committed probe.

1. WHERE A WRITE-BACK'S TIME GOES (fd5ae9b, 200,000 events)
Plain: 19,939 issues, 88,152 events known (all named), 200,000 ids. Ownership-heavy (fd5ae9b, before PR #33): 14,578 issues, 51,594 known.
| phase | made by project() | decoded + 1 comment | compacting (decoded + 1) | ownership, decoded + 1 |
| texts (Here issues' texts) | 33.1 ms, 3.62 MB | 0.19 ms, 2 KB | 0.19 ms | 0.16 ms |
| named | - | - | 18.9 ms | (16.1 compacting) |
| kept (Knowledge::kept) | - | - | 26.3 ms | (13.9 compacting) |
| issues (write_issue x every issue) | 36.4 ms, 7.18 MB (360 B an issue) | 20.7 ms, 7.18 MB | 21.3 ms | 33.3 ms, 8.33 MB (572 B an issue) |
| state rest (by_key, renames, integrity, pending, counters, last_by_thread) | 0.94 ms, 0.51 MB | 0.80 ms | 0.83 ms | 0.33 ms, 0.37 MB |
| asked() + writers + chain breaks | 2.4 ms, 3 KB | 2.5 ms | 2.6 ms | 1.7 ms |
| event records (id, deps, machine, actor) | 21.0 ms, 3.31 MB (37.6 B an event) | 15.2 ms, 3.31 MB | 15.8 ms | 8.1 ms, 2.88 MB (55.9 B) |
| applicable + ancestry (places, clocks, sets, arena) | 2.3 ms, 2.24 MB | 2.3 ms | 2.3 ms | 1.8 ms, 1.78 MB |
| heads + ids | 0.74 ms, 3.20 MB | 1.8 ms | 2.0 ms | 2.7 ms, 3.20 MB |
| index rest (lengths, lasts, superseded, open) | 0.003 ms | 0.004 ms | 0.004 ms | 1.0 ms, 0.72 MB (superseded) |
| encode, whole | 98 ms | 43.4 ms | ~90 ms | 45.6 ms |
| sum state + index (16.4 MB) | | 6.4 ms | | 6.8 ms |
| assemble into one Vec (file::bytes) | | 1.8 ms | | 2.0 ms |
| write + rename 16.4 MB | | 5.1 ms | | 4.9 ms |
| Projection::decode / decode_state | 124 / 59 ms | | | 100 / 54 ms |
| texts read in + extend by one comment | 0.25 ms | | | 0.19 ms |
Parts at 200,000 (plain): state 7.69 MB (issues 7.18, the rest 0.51), index 8.75 MB (event records 3.31, ancestry 2.24, ids 3.20), texts file 3.62 MB; the file 16.46 MB. Names: 21 in the state part, 6 in the index; shared values 6-12 and 6 (the synthetic histories have few writers; a real tracker has one actor per agent thread). At 20,000 (plain, 1,990 issues, 8,850 known): decoded + 1 encodes in 2.8 ms (issues 1.3, event records 0.8, ancestry 0.3, ids 0.2, writers 0.2), sums 0.6 ms, write 0.5 ms; parts 0.77 / 0.83 MB.
The copy step 4 would do instead, simulated on the same bytes (each issue's range and each event record's range copied by offset into a new Vec, with a u32 offset table): issues 0.37 ms, event records 0.39 ms at 200,000 plain; 0.79 and 0.27 ms ownership-heavy.
End to end (timing --read, best of three runs, fd5ae9b): 200,000: list 0.090 s, show 0.082 s, write after a read 0.156 s, read after a write 0.193 s, write after a write 0.152 s; 20,000: 13.5, 12.9, 29.6, 23.4, 29.5 ms. timing --sync 200000 (one run): a sync after a local write 0.281 s, a write published at once 0.528 s.
So a read after a write at 200,000 pays about 110 ms over a plain read: the index decode (~65 ms: Projection::decode 124 against decode_state 59), the encode (43 ms), sums, assembling and writing (13 ms). X17's 94 ms encode (ec773f9) is 43 ms now: step 3 took the compaction out (45 ms), and an issue whose texts are only in the file (its Stored cloned) encodes in about 1.0 us where one whose texts are Here (a fresh projection) takes 1.8 us (summary() computed). Of the 43 ms, 36 ms are the issues and the event records: what step 4 copies.

2. WHAT AN ISSUE'S AND AN EVENT RECORD'S BYTES DEPEND ON OUTSIDE THEM TODAY
- Writer::name: the state part's names (an issue's origin machine, its claim's owner, machine, agent, thread and mode, offline claimants, edge kinds, the ended-by of Stored.ended after #33, the writers' machines) are written inline the first time and as number + 1 after, in one table for the whole part; the index's (event records' machines) likewise. An issue's bytes refer to names an earlier issue defined: re-encoding one issue renumbers every later one.
- Writer::shared: the same for shared values (actors, places, where_, closed_on, claim and offline places), keyed by the Arc's address, not its content: two equal values held by different Arcs are two entries, and the numbers depend on which Arcs the issues hold.
- Text places: an issue's record holds its texts' place (at, len, sum) in the text file, given by encode for texts Here (written anew), and Stored (tags, disputed, ended) recomputed by summary() for texts Read. A record depends on the text file's offsets and generation.
- The writers section depends on every issue's registers (asked(): the events behind registers with several entries, over all issues) and is filtered over every event the knowledge holds: O(issues + events) at every write-back, whatever changed.
- by_key is written beside the issues though it is the issues' keys in issue order (create inserts both; nothing else touches it): 0.5 MB and 0.8 ms of every write-back.
- Event records: the machine and actor through the index's tables. Their place and clock are not in the record but in the ancestry's arrays, indexed by the event's position; clocks point into the shared positions arena and the sets.
- Derived on decode, never written: labels, children, awaiting (finish() in read_state), so relabelling and the parent-child index change no bytes.
- Order: an issue's place in the IndexMap (creation order), an event's in the knowledge (journal order, its index the ancestry's).
WHAT PR #33 CHANGES (read on ownership-history-with-texts, 337b752, not yet restacked onto fd5ae9b): the ended claims, lost claims and stale ends leave write_issue/read_issue for the texts (write_history in write_texts, its own Writer, so self-contained as all texts are); the issue keeps its current claim, generation and offline claims, and Stored gains ended (who ended the last claim, a name, and how). Claims, releases, closes and reopens now need the issue's texts read in (texts_in: needs, not changes) and mark them changed only when the history grows: Issue::ended/lost/ignored call history_changed(), Read -> Here. That is the mark pattern step 4 generalises, and it moves the ownership-heavy history's bytes (8.33 MB of issues at 200,000) out of what step 4 copies. It adds a name to each issue record (ended.by) and leaves the layout's dependencies as above.

3. EVERY PATH THAT CHANGES AN ISSUE OR AN EVENT RECORD BETWEEN A DECODE AND AN ENCODE, AND ITS MARK
Every encode is the store's save, in current(), after decode -> set_texts_file -> about/read_texts -> extend -> save (or after project()); Tx's own extensions and a merge's go through current() or are never encoded. Within that:
a. apply_one on the event's issue: updated_at (unless imported), where_; then the operation: set (registers, stamps own_*), claim/release/close/delete/reopen (claim, generation, offline claims, status and assignee registers, closed_on, extra for a delete, the history: texts after #33), comment (comments: texts; comment_count: global), dep_add/dep_remove (dep_tags, retracted; awaiting.retract takes the issue's own dangling entries), labels (label_tags). Mark: through the issue accessor (below). Also orphans, last_by_thread, comment_count: globals, re-encoded.
b. A create: the new issue (appended: beyond what is stored), by_key, renames (a copy renamed), and each issue awaiting its key (awaiting.arrived, then bind on another issue: dep_tags, dangling taken out). Mark: the accessor (create.rs takes st.issues.get_mut for the other issue).
c. finish_some: settle_awaiting (dangling lists made whole on the issues taken from: already marked by b or a), relabel (labels: derived, no bytes), index_children (derived).
d. Texts: texts_in sets Read -> Here for issues an event changes the texts of (and, after #33, history_changed does when an ownership event grows the history); a Here issue gets a new place at encode. Mark: encode treats every issue with Texts::Here as changed, whatever its marks: a new place is a new record.
e. Texts read in (State::read_texts, by the store's read_texts and about): There -> Read(place), the registers reordered as the texts were written. The record is unchanged if summary(issue, place) == the stored Stored and the non-text registers keep their order. This path must not mark (a show or an export reads in every text), so it alone takes a non-marking accessor, and the tests check its claim byte for byte (5).
f. save's anew path (more of the text file no longer read than read): every text read in, write_texts_anew sets every issue Here: every record changes; a fresh encode.
g. placed() after encode (Here -> Read): after the bytes are written; nothing encodes after.
h. add_unconfirmed (the store's view): after current() returns, never encoded; the accessor marks anyway.
i. Event records: Knowledge::push appends (extend); observe_one records the new event's place and clock and touches only chain_breaks, applicable and the chains' lengths/last (small, re-encoded). An existing event's record (id, deps, machine, actor) and its place and clock never change between compactions: the decoded events are a prefix of the encoded ones. No marks are needed for them, only that prefix property, which the tests check. A compaction (Knowledge::kept, at encode when compaction_due) renumbers everything: the index is encoded fresh then.
j. The rest of the index: heads, lengths, lasts: re-encoded; ids: advance is the only path that adds any (a batch's go in where they sort), and it keeps the list of those it added since the decode, for encode to merge into the stored run: that list is the ids' mark; superseded and open never change in an extension (takeovers and batches that would leave something waiting are declined), so they can be copied.
k. A merge, info, machines: current() with Want::Projection: the same paths as a, b, d, i. A merge that replays: project(), nothing stored, a fresh encode.
The mark: State's issues become a newtype (Issues) that derefs to the IndexMap for reading and mutates only through methods: get_mut marks the issue's position, values_mut marks all, insert appends (beyond what is stored), read_in (for State::read_texts alone) does not mark. A missed mark then needs a mutable path that does not go through Issues, which the compiler refuses, or a misused read_in; encode adds "Texts::Here is changed". The marks are a bitset over the positions the stored bytes hold, cleared at the end of decode (read_state's finish relabels every issue through values_mut). A wrong mark costs a copy; a missed one copies stale bytes, which the next decode reads as current: hence the oracle in 5 on every path.

4. THE LAYOUT (step 4; one projection::ENCODING bump, the store's file layout unchanged: one file, made + state + index, renamed whole)
State part (what decode_state reads): (1) its table: names (count, texts) and shared values (count, values), each entry referred to by its number alone, never defined inline; (2) prefix, name; (3) the issues, each record self-contained but for table numbers and its texts' place: as today's write_issue (after #33) plus the writers of its registers with several entries (event id, machine, actor), which replaces the global writers section and asked() (every writer is the issue's own event: a register holds only events applied to its issue); a state read alone then lists its writers (State::events, State::holds) in issue order, not the journal's, which no command asks and known.rs compares as a set; (4) renames, integrity, pending, orphans, comment_count, last_by_thread, chain breaks (small, re-encoded each time). by_key is not written: decode makes it from the issues, as it makes awaiting.
Index part (what Projection::decode reads after it): (1) its table: names and shared values, and the ancestry's chain sets and positions arena, all append-only between compactions; (2) the event records, each: id, deps, machine, actor, place, clock (set, arena start): everything per event in one record, the ancestry's per-event arrays gone; (3) machines, applicable, the chains' sequenced/lengths/last, compacted, heads, ids (one ascending run), lengths, lasts, superseded, open.
No offset table is stored: decode reads the records in order and records where each issue began (a Vec<u32>, 80 KB at 200,000), and where the event records, sets and arena end. A stored table would be bytes to validate and nothing more in step 4; step 5's root gets one.
What decode keeps to copy from: the parts as read (the store moves its Encoded into Projection::decode, held as an Arc so a clone shares it), the issue offsets, the table sizes. Cost: the 16.4 MB the store read are held from the decode to the write-back instead of freed after it, at 200,000 (1.6 MB at 20,000). The store lets go of them when current() returns (a write keeps its transaction to exit, not the bytes). At the write-back, today's peak (projection + new parts + the assembled copy file::bytes makes) becomes projection + kept + new parts once file::bytes writes the header and parts through write_cache_parts as parts (it takes a list already): the same peak. Measured on fd5ae9b at 200,000 (cargo xtask bead, on the timing --read store): a list 51 MB, a write 88 MB, the read after a write, which writes back, 103 MB (118 MB the first time after a sync). Prediction for step 4: the list and the write unchanged (decode_state keeps nothing; a write lets go of the bytes before its transaction starts), the write-back within its Vecs' slack of 103 MB (today the parts grow by doubling; a copying encode knows their sizes and reserves them); measured in the PR, not assumed.
Encode, when there is something to copy from: the state table written whole (the stored entries, then those this write-back added); every stored issue unmarked and not Here copied from its range; every other issue written against the table (names looked up by content, values by address first and then by content, so a value equal to a stored one does not get a second entry); the rest written. The index, when it does not compact: the table, sets and arena as stored plus what was added; the stored event records copied as one range plus the new ones written; ids merged as ranges of the stored run between the batch's ids (16 bytes each, fixed width: no per-id work); the rest written. A fresh encode (everything written, the tables made anew from what is referenced) when there is nothing stored (project()), when the knowledge compacts (index only: event records are renumbered), when every text is written anew (state part), or when the state table holds more than an eighth more entries than when it was last made fresh (a count in the state part; the index's table is bounded by its compaction).
Expected encode at 200,000: copies ~0.8 ms + the issues and events marked + the small rest (~1-2 ms) = about 2-3 ms where it is 43 ms; leaving the writers, by_key and the ancestry out of it would leave about 8 ms.
decode_state: the same work in a different order (the table read before the issues instead of inline; a number per reference as now; by_key cloned from the issue's key instead of read: one String either way); it must not be slower, and timing --decode will say so.

5. HOW THE TESTS SEE A MISSED MARK, BEFORE ANYTHING CHANGES
First commit, tests only, green on main once #33 is on it (the layout the step builds on): projection/tests/marked.rs.
- record_of(issue): the issue's record written alone, with a fresh Writer (names and values inline: deterministic by content), its texts' place as encode would write it (a Here issue a place no record has).
- At every read_back (the decode the differential tracks take, and the deferred track's), the baseline: every issue's record_of by position, and the decoded knowledge's event records (id, deps, machine, actor, place, clock) by position.
- After every extension (each track, the deferred track, the flawed histories), changed(baseline, projection): the issues at stored positions whose record_of differs, and whether any baseline event record differs or moved. Checks: changed issues are among the marked ones, and no baseline event record changed unless the knowledge was compacted since. On today's code marked() is every issue (today's encode writes them all, which is the honest mark of the code as it is), so the check passes; the step's code replaces it with the projection's own marks, and then it bites.
- A tally of what changed and how, with minima the generator must reach (enough()): issues changed as the event's own issue, by a set, an ownership event, a delete, a comment, an edge; another issue bound by a create's key; a copy renamed; texts re-placed; an issue only read in and unchanged (path e); event records appended between compactions and rewritten by one. Where a path is drawn too rarely, the draw code gets a function of its own (the edges' drawn.rs is the model), with the generator-only commit first and every pinned answer re-made on it if the histories change.
- Self-tests: changing one field of one issue, or an event's record, is seen.
Second commit (marks, no layout change): Issues and its marks; marked() becomes the projection's. A tightness check too: an issue only read in is not marked (so a read that reads every text does not quietly re-encode everything).
Layout and copy commits: read_back also encodes fresh (encode_with a test-only "copy nothing") and asserts that both decode alike and that each issue the encode copied has the bytes write_issue gives it now against the same table, naming the seed, batch and issue otherwise.
Mutations I will show failing, each with the test that fails:
1. apply_one's updated_at through the non-marking accessor (an issue changed, unmarked).
2. create.rs's bind on an awaited issue through it (another issue changed, unmarked).
3. An event record changed: an existing event's actor rewritten in extend; and a push before the end.
4. A stale name number: the seeded name map off by one.
5. A stale shared-value number: the address map off by one, and the content lookup dropped (a value appended twice).
6. The offsets off by one record (issue i copied from i+1's start).
7. Texts Here copied (the Here rule dropped).
8. A compaction that copies the event records anyway.
9. An id of the batch left out of the merged run.
10. The state table never made fresh (a bound on its entries fails: a test with many distinct actors).
11. read_texts marking (the tightness check fails: a speed-up lost, not an answer).
12. by_key made from the issues in another order, or a renamed copy's key left out.
Plus the existing differential, flawed, deferred and many_seeds runs, each comparing with replay after every write-back.

6. STEP 5 ON THIS LAYOUT (roll-lqjj.45)
Files: <store>/projection becomes the root, still renamed whole (write_cache_parts); the records go to <store>/projection-records, append-only like the text file: a header (magic, generation: the sum of the bytes it was started with), appended under its own lock at its length, started again (renamed whole) when it holds more bytes no longer placed than an eighth of those placed (tighter than the text file's "more than read, plus 1 MiB", because every decode, a list's included, reads and sums the live records), and at a compaction of the knowledge or a fresh state table, which rewrite most records anyway. Texts stay in their own file: a list never reads them.
What goes in the records file: a start-again lays the base out in kind order, the state half first (state table, issue records) and the index half after (index table, sets, arena, event records, ids); each write-back then appends one extent, its own state half (the state table's added entries, the issue records written: marked, Here, new) and index half (the index table's added entries, sets and arena positions, the new event records, the batch's ids as an ascending run), each half placed and summed apart by the root. Weighed and not chosen: the records in the text file itself (one file, one lock, one argument), since a list would then read past texts it never prints.
The root: header and sums as now; made (build, journal files, the text file's generation and the records file's); the state's small rest (prefix, name, renames, integrity, pending, counters, last_by_thread, chain breaks); the issue table (each issue's offset and length in the records file, in issue order: ~8 B an issue, 160 KB at 200,000); every live extent (at, len, sum, kind); the index's small rest (machines, applicable, chains, compacted, heads, lengths, lasts, superseded, open). About 0.2-0.3 MB at 200,000 where the file is 16.4 MB (X17's ~1 MB assumed the ancestry and by_key stayed in it).
Reading: decode_state reads the root, then the base's state half and the appended tail (two reads, not a read an extent), sums the state halves, and parses the issue records at the root's offsets; Projection::decode reads and sums the index halves too, the id runs merged (concatenated, sorted, refused if not distinct). Decode keeps nothing of the bytes: an untouched record stays where it is, so step 4's held copy goes and so does the write-back's new 16 MB.
The durability argument (REVIEWING section 2, roll-lqjj.27) must then cover a third file, needed by every decode where texts are needed only by some commands:
- Interrupted between the append and the root's rename (failpoint projection.records-appended, and atomic-write on the root): the old root stands; the appended bytes are unplaced, garbage the next append goes after (always at the file's length) and the rule above counts.
- Two processes writing back at once: appends are serialized by the records file's lock, held through the root's rename as save holds the text file's now (the text file's lock taken first, always, so two savers cannot deadlock), so a root names only extents written before it, its own included; the last rename wins and the other's extents are garbage. A process whose lock outlived a start-again appended to the unlinked file: its root names the old generation and is refused, a replay.
- A root whose sums do not match: no projection, as now. A root whose sums match but whose extents a crash lost, zeroed or cut (the rename reached the disk before the append did): an extent's sum fails, so the decode fails and the journal is replayed; unlike a text, a record is needed by every command, so it costs a replay at the next command rather than at the next command that prints the text. A records file of another generation: the same.
- Readers against writers: a reader takes only what the root it read places, all of it written before that root, never rewritten (appends only); a start-again between its root and its open shows another generation: a replay, rarely.
- The text file's argument is unchanged; the pairings (root newer, older, another generation, one without the other) get the same treatment for the records file, and the tests (projection::tests, the black-box storage::projection with a bead killed between the append and the rename, and every pairing of root, records and text file) must say so.
Should step 4's layout change so that step 5 needs no second change of the records' bytes? Yes, and the layout in 4 is chosen for it: each event record carries its place and clock (else the ancestry's 2.2 MB stay in the root or need their own format change); records refer to tables by absolute number and never define entries inline; nothing in a record is relative to where it sits; writers ride in the issue records and by_key is derived (else they stay in the root). Step 5 then changes the root and where the records sit, not their bytes; one ENCODING bump each.

7. EXPECTED GAINS AND COSTS
Step 4, 200,000 events, plain: a write-back's encode 43 ms -> about 3 ms (8 ms if writers, by_key and the ancestry were left as they are); timing --read: read after a write 0.193 s -> about 0.155 s; write after a read 0.156 s and write after a write 0.152 s unchanged (they do not write back below the 64th; the write that crosses it gains the 40 ms); list, show, ready unchanged (decode_state the same work); --sync: unchanged but for its write-backs (the merge writes back only past the 64th). Ownership-heavy (fd5ae9b): encode 45.6 -> about 5 ms; after #33 the issues are smaller and both figures will be re-measured. 20,000: encode 2.8 -> about 0.5 ms, read after a write 23.4 -> about 21 ms; nothing else moves. Bytes: -0.5 MB (by_key) of 16.4 MB; the tables grow by what write-backs add between fresh encodes, an eighth at most. Heap: +16.4 MB held from decode to write-back at 200,000 (1.6 MB at 20,000), the peak unchanged once the assembled copy goes.
Step 5, 200,000: a write-back writes about 0.3 MB (root) + ~1-2 KB appended instead of 16.4 MB: sums 6.4 -> ~0.2 ms, assembling 1.8 -> 0, writing 5.1 -> ~0.2 ms: about -12 ms (read after a write -> about 0.143 s); 20,000 about -1.1 ms. Reads read and sum up to an eighth more record bytes before a start-again. Heap: step 4's held copy and the write-back's 16.4 MB of new parts go. A start-again of the records file rewrites everything once every (live / 8) / (bytes a write-back appends) write-backs: about 2 MB / 0.5 KB, some thousands at 200,000, besides the ones a knowledge compaction brings.
What X17's design missed or got wrong, now measured:
- The encode is 43 ms on fd5ae9b, not 94: step 3 took 45 ms; the issues are 20.7 ms of a decoded projection (49 was a fresh one, every texts' summary computed), the event records 15.2 ms (not 21). Step 4's gain is ~40 ms, not 50-70.
- Event records need no marks and no offset table: between compactions they are append-only and never change (Knowledge::push), so they are one range copied; at a compaction they are renumbered and written fresh.
- The ancestry (2.2 MB, 2.3 ms) is per event and append-only too: it belongs in the event records, or step 5's root is 2 MB, not 1.
- The writers section and asked() are O(issues + events) at every write-back (2.5 ms), and by_key (0.5 MB, 0.8 ms) is derivable: both go.
- The shared-value table is keyed by the Arc's address: copying needs it content-stable.
- Keeping the stored bytes costs 16.4 MB of heap at 200,000 unless the assembled copy goes; step 5 removes the need.
- Step 5's records file must compact tighter than the text file, because every decode reads it.
- After steps 4 and 5 the read after a write still pays ~65 ms at 200,000 to decode the index and ~0.3 ms to extend: the option X17 rejected, a write writing back its own projection, cost a 106 ms write-back in the write then; after step 4 it costs ~3 ms of encode and 13 ms of sums and writing, ~1 ms of those after step 5, and would make the read after a write a plain read (0.08-0.09 s). I recommend the orchestrator weigh it as a step after 5 (its lock and crash questions are those of a write-back today); I do not plan it in .44 or .45.
Risk: medium-high for step 4 (a missed mark is a stale answer until the next replay; the Issues newtype and the oracle are the defence); high for step 5 (a third file in the crash argument).

What step 5 takes from step 4's design (br-copy, full design on roll-lqjj.44): step 4 makes every issue record and every event record self-contained but for table numbers (the names and shared values, and the ancestry's chain sets and positions arena, in tables of their own, append-only between fresh encodes), puts each event's place and clock in its record, moves the writers into the issue records and derives by_key, so that step 5 changes where the records sit and the root, never the records' bytes. Step 5: <store>/projection becomes a small root renamed whole (made, the state's and index's small rest, the issue table of offsets, every live extent with its sum; about 0.2-0.3 MB at 200,000 events where the file is 16.4 MB on fd5ae9b), and the records go to <store>/projection-records, append-only under its own lock (taken after the text file's, held through the root's rename), one extent per write-back with a state half and an index half summed apart, started again when it holds more bytes no longer placed than an eighth of those placed (tighter than the text file, since every decode reads it). Measured on fd5ae9b at 200,000: summing 6.4 ms, assembling 1.8 ms and writing 5.1 ms of every write-back, about 12 ms of what step 5 removes, and the 16.4 MB step 4 holds to copy from. The durability bullet must then cover a third file needed by every decode: an append without its root (garbage, appended after), two writers (serialized by the lock, last rename wins), a root whose extents a crash lost (a sum fails, a replay at the next command), another generation, and every pairing of root, records and text file, with failpoint and black-box kill tests.

data.text: Audit: a prune after the fetch also breaks the merge's reads. A fetched subtree or segment blob gone from sync.git answers GIT_ERROR ('git ls-tree -r: error: Could not read', 'git cat-file blob: bad file'), and so does every later sync: the next fetch finds the tip already under refs/beads/remote and brings nothing. Fix in link/read.rs: a failed read of the fetched tip (manifest, listing, blob) asks what of it is missing or damaged (local_damage of git's message, cat-file -e of the tip, rev-list --objects --no-walk --missing=print, which skips gitlinks) and reports that through Link::damage, so the command makes sync.git again. A whole tree without a manifest blob stays MANIFEST_MISSING; a gitlink where a segment goes stays GIT_ERROR. The push side was probed with push.before (the publish's new blob or commit pruned before the push): the push is rejected, the next round publishes, no change needed.

fields.description: Found while designing roll-lqjj.45. fs::written_whole writes .NAME.PID.tmp beside its target and removes it only when the write or rename returns an error; a bead killed between the create and the rename (a sigkill, a crash, the atomic-write failpoint with sigkill) leaves it, and no later process removes it, since the name holds the dead process's id. For the projection that is a file the size of the projection (15.6 MB at 200,000 events) per kill, in the store, never read. Step 5's records file would add one more such target. A fix would remove stale .*.tmp files of the store's cache files (projection, projection-texts) under the lock that writes them, or name the temporary file so the next writer reuses it.

THE FILES
1. `<store>/projection` becomes the root. It is still renamed whole (write_cache_parts), and holds:
   - the header and its sums;
   - made: build, journal files, the text file's generation and the records file's;
   - the state's rest: prefix, name, renames, integrity, pending, orphans, counts, last_by_thread, chain breaks;
   - the index's rest: chains, compacted, heads, lengths, lasts, superseded, open;
   - the list of extents.

2. `<store>/projection-records`. It starts with a header (magic, and the generation, which is the sum of its base), then:
   - The base, written at a start-again, laid out by kind:
     - the state half: the table, the issue records, an offset table (4 B an issue, 80 KB at 200,000), and by_key;
     - the index half: the table, the event records, places, clocks, chain sets, positions, and the ids.
   - Then the extents, one per write-back, each with two halves:
     - its state half: the table entries added, the issue records written (marked, Here, new; each with its position, or "new"), and the keys added;
     - its index half: the table entries added, the event records, places, clocks, sets and positions added, and the batch's ids as an ascending run.

The bytes of the records do not change: step 4 already made them refer to tables by number, never relative to where they sit. Step 5 is one ENCODING (12) and one LAYOUT change.

Where by_key and the ancestry columns go: into the records file, as append-only sub-columns of the base and of each extent, beside the records they belong with.
- Between compactions and fresh tables they only grow at their end. Step 4 copies each as one prefix and its byte oracle pins it; mutation 12 fails 41 tests.
- In the root, they would cost 2.75 MB at 200,000: keys 0.51 + places 0.41 + clocks 0.44 + arena 1.39. That is rewritten and summed at every write-back (about 2.5 ms of sums and 1.1 ms of writing), and by_key would be read by every list anyway.
- In the records file, they add no bytes to the root and no reads: they sit in the same spans a decode reads already. A decode parses each column in at most 65 fragments (the base and up to 64 extents).

Root size:
- At 200,000 plain: made 22 KB (207 segments), each rest under 0.5 KB, and the extent list at most 64 x about 100 B = 6.4 KB. That is at most about 29 KB, where the projection file is 15.64 MB today.
- At 20,000: made 2.6 KB, so at most about 9.5 KB.
- made scales with the journal's files whatever step 5 does (an ownership-heavy store's attempt files).

Considered and not chosen: the issue table in the root.
- It would cost 8 B an issue: 160 KB at 200,000, rewritten and summed at every write-back.
- The base's offset table plus each extent's positions give the same lookup, and nothing is rewritten.

A decode's reads:
- decode_state makes 3 preads:
  - the root, whole, summed;
  - the base state half, summed;
  - the tail, everything after the base in one read; only its state halves are summed.
- Projection::decode reads the root, the whole base and the tail, and sums all of them.
- Live issue records are found through the offset table, with each extent's positions applied, and only they are parsed. A dead record is read and summed but never parsed. Building that table costs O(issues + records in extents), about 0.02 ms.
- Ids: each run is checked ascending and inserted into the set it is read into. A duplicate across runs is refused, so nothing is merged.
- Decode keeps nothing of the bytes: step 4's Kept goes.

Starting the records file again. Whichever save meets one of these rules does it:
(a) it would hold more than 64 extents;
(b) the dead bytes of the state halves (replaced records and garbage) would exceed a 32nd of the live state bytes, or all dead bytes would exceed an eighth of the live bytes;
(c) a knowledge compaction (events renumbered) or a fresh state table (records renumbered);
(d) a projection made whole by replay, or no usable records file (missing, another generation, not openable, failing a sum).

Rule (a) bounds a decode's fragments and the list of extents. In practice it decides first: a comment's write-back leaves about 320 B dead (one issue record), so 64 write-backs leave about 20 KB.

The cost of a start-again:
- After (a) to (c): the live bytes are read back from the records file the save just decoded (page cache) and copied as step 4 copies them, then summed and written. That is about 14-16 ms at 200,000, today's write-back, once every 64 write-backs or fewer: about 0.25 ms a write-back amortized.
- After (d): a whole encode, as a replay's save does today.

1. LOCKS
Recommended: one lock file, `<store>/projection.lock`, never renamed, taken exclusive by save for:
- appending texts;
- appending records;
- starting either file again;
- renaming the root.

Why it replaces the text file's own lock: that lock is on an inode a start-again renames away.
- A saver that waited on it holds a lock on a file that is no longer at the path. For texts, the raced test of #36 pins that it then writes nothing, or every text anew.
- For the records file, the same staleness would let a root name an old generation, so every command would replay until the next save.
- A lock file that is never renamed makes that impossible.

Order: the store lock (when held), then projection.lock. Nothing takes them the other way round.
- Readers take no lock on their read path.
- A reader's write-back takes projection.lock alone.
- A writer's write-back past the 64th runs inside its transaction or merge, which hold the store lock, so it takes projection.lock second.

Who appends, and when: every save that is not a start-again. These are exactly today's callers:
- a reading command that applied records (current(), any want but Projection);
- a write whose applied records pass a 64th of the projection (kept_for);
- the save after a replay always starts the file again (rule d).
Nothing else writes either file.

roll-lqjj.51 (not planned):
- A write writing back its own projection would be one more save caller, taking projection.lock in the same order. Better, it would take it after the store lock is released: a save needs only projection.lock, as a reader's does, so .51 need not lengthen the store lock.
- Nothing in this design makes .51 harder. With step 5, .51's per-write cost falls from about 14.6 ms to about 0.5 ms at 200,000 (below).

Another build of bead beside this one (an upgrade mid-session) still locks the text file, so its appends could interleave with this build's.
- Each root is its own build's (made.build), so no root is trusted across builds.
- Texts written over fail their sums and replay. The answer is never wrong.
- This goes in REVIEWING §2 with the change.

2. STARTING AGAIN, AND A READER IN BETWEEN
The start-again, all under projection.lock:
1. Write the new records file as `.projection-records.PID.tmp`.
2. Rename it over projection-records.
3. Write and rename the root.

A reader then sees one of three things:
- the old root and the old file, if it opened the file before step 2 (its fd keeps the old inode): consistent;
- the new root and the new file: consistent;
- the old root and the new file: the header names another generation.

A reader retries on a mismatch once before it replays:
- It takes projection.lock shared. That blocks only while a save holds the lock, and a start-again holds it from before step 2 until after step 3.
- Under the lock it reads the root and the records again, then lets go.
- The retry costs one more decode's reads (3-60 ms at 200,000) against a replay's 2.76 s. It happens only on a mismatch, so the common path takes no lock.
- If the retry mismatches too, no saver is in the middle: a crash between steps 2 and 3. The reader replays, and its save starts the file again (rule d).

A writer under the store lock that meets a mismatch takes projection.lock shared second, which keeps the order.

3. CRASH POINTS
Each gets a failpoint and a black-box test in crates/beadroll/tests/cli/storage/projection/, its machine rust_only, plus in-crate projection tests.

a. An append without its root.
   - Failpoint: `projection.records-appended`, after the extent is written and before the root is written, with sigkill.
   - Effect: the old root names what it named, and the extent is garbage at the file's end. The next save appends after it (always at the file's length) and counts it dead.
   - Test: kill a show's write-back there. list and show then answer as a replay of the journal does; the next write-back writes a new root, and the file has grown past the garbage.

b. A root renamed before its append reached the disk (an unflushed append lost under a root that survived).
   - Failpoint: a new action, `lose`, at `projection.records-append`. It reports the append written and writes nothing; the root is then renamed.
   - Test 1: the next command finds the root naming bytes past the file's end. The read fails, it replays, and answers alike.
   - Test 2: another save appends at that offset first, so the bytes there are another extent's. The first root is put back as a lost rename would leave it. Its extent's sum fails, and it replays.

c. A torn append.
   - Failpoint: `projection.records-append=torn-sigkill`, as `append.mid` does: half the extent written and fsynced, then killed. No root names it, so it is garbage, as in (a).
   - Variant: a new action, `torn`, writes half and goes on to write the root. The root's extent sum fails, and it replays.

d. A start-again interrupted.
   - Failpoint: the existing `atomic-written:projection-records` with sigkill: the new file is renamed and the root is not.
     - Effect: the old root and the new file mismatch, the retry finds no saver, the command replays, and its save starts the file again.
     - Test: the answers, and the generations before and after.
   - Failpoint: `atomic-write:projection-records` with sigkill, before the rename.
     - Effect: the old pair stands and the temporary file is left behind. That is true of every atomic write today, so I recorded it as roll-lqjj.52 (below).

- Every pairing of root, records file and text file: newer, older, another generation, missing.
- `a_damaged_projection_is_never_trusted` (every cut, a flipped byte every seventh) extended to the records file.

4. DURABILITY (REVIEWING §2's durability bullet, roll-lqjj.27; X05)
Nothing in the records file is trusted for being there either. Point 2 of the bullet, a text never read on its file's say-so, applies to every record, with the root as the projection.

What an unflushed append under a flushed root can leave after a power loss:
- the extent missing: the file is shorter, so the read fails;
- zeroed or holed (blocks allocated, data not written): the sum fails;
- stale bytes from reused blocks: the sum fails;
- partly written: the sum fails;
- whole: the root is right.

The reverse case, an older root that survived beside a newer records file (the rename lost, the appends kept):
- It names only extents written before it, whose bytes are the ones it summed. That makes it a whole projection bead wrote at an earlier moment, judged against the journal's files as point 1 says.
- A root of another generation than the file's: a replay.

So in every state a crash leaves:
- either every byte a root names sums to what that root recorded, which makes it exactly what bead wrote with it (a true projection of the journal at that moment);
- or the decode fails, and the journal is replayed (2.76 s at 200,000, once per crash).
The sums are 128-bit (two SipHash-1-3 halves), against accidental damage, as today.

Why no fsync is still right:
- Measured on this machine (ext4 on dm-crypt), an append of 1.5 KB plus a 27 KB root through a rename takes 0.09 ms plain and 33.7 ms with both fsynced (median of 40).
- That is more than twice what step 5 saves, at a cost that only buys skipping a replay after a power loss. That is X05's argument again, and stronger.
- I propose no fsync.

5. A HOSTILE OR CORRUPT RECORDS FILE
It is refused whole, never a panic. The checks:
- the root's lengths add up to its size;
- at most 64 extents, ascending, not overlapping, each within the records file (checked_add throughout);
- each half's sum;
- the offset table's entries ascending, within the base's state half;
- each extent's positions within the issue count, none twice in one extent;
- each record parses to exactly the end of its slot;
- the id runs ascending, and distinct across runs;
- every count bounded by the bytes left, as Reader::count already does.

The fuzz target `segment` gains a (root, records) input, split by the input's first byte.

A file with right sums and wrong content is what a hostile projection is today. Whoever can write the store can write its journal.

WHERE AND WHEN
- The write-back runs in beadroll-sync's `written` (writes.rs) once `locked` has returned, so the store lock is released first. It takes only the text file's lock, through the store's `save`, as a reader's write-back does. A writer's critical section grows only by the step that names its files (below, about 0.3 ms).
- It runs before the answer is printed, for three reasons:
  - A write published at once publishes in `cli::finish` before it prints, and its merge should find the stored projection current, not extend it again.
  - A caller that starts its next command as soon as it reads the answer would otherwise race the write-back and lose the gain.
  - One path serves every write.
  The process's total time is the same either way. The time to the first output is later by the write-back (about 15 ms at 200,000 events).

WHAT `made` NAMES
- The transaction keeps the basis its projection was read with: the store's `Made` (with every file's identity and sum), handed out through `Sourced` as an opaque `Basis`. `Tx::new` and `Tx::on` both get it.
- After the append, still under the store lock, `beadroll_store::after_write` lists the journal as `current` does and accepts it only if:
  - every segment and attempt file other than this write's has the identity the basis gives it;
  - this machine's active segment either grew from the basis's length (the bytes before still sum to the basis's sum), or is a new segment after the last;
  - the bytes it gained parse to exactly the events the write appended, by id and in order. The new identity and the sum of the whole segment are then taken. A segment holds at most 256 KB plus one batch, so this costs at most about 0.3 ms.
  - for an ownership write whose attempt counted here (offline, no remote, or accepted online), the one new attempt file holds exactly its events. Its identity and the sum of its bytes are taken.
- Anything else means no write-back, and the next command does what it does today. That covers a file changed by anything else (`published`, a merge, a repaired tail), and an attempt still pending, whose events are in the projection but not yet in the journal.

WHICH WRITES
- Every write through `written` (writing, writing_state, writing_spent): create, comments, dep, close, reopen, delete, update, import.
- Offline or local ownership commands, which use `writing`.
- Online ownership rounds (`coordinated`): claim and release write back after the round, once its lock is released, with the basis their merge's projection had.
- A takeover, and a machine's first record, leave the transaction with a replayed state and no projection. They write nothing back, and the next command extends or replays as today.
- A write published at once writes back before its publish. The publish's merge then finds the stored projection current. It extends and writes back, under the 64th rule as today, only what the fetch brought.

The 64th rule (kept_for):
- A merge, `info` and `machines` keep it unchanged.
- A transaction still reads with it. When the records left after the stored projection pass a 64th, `current` writes back inside the transaction's read, as today, and the write writes back again after its append. That is rare: it happens after a crash, an older bead, or a merge that wrote nothing back.
- A write that appended nothing writes nothing back after.
- A run of writes now writes back at every write. That is the cost the maintainer accepted, and step 5 is what would remove it.

A READ AFTER A WRITE
- A read after a write is a plain read when the journal's files are the ones the projection names.
- One case needs care. The write appends and then writes back within a few milliseconds, so its segment's times can fall in the stored projection's own timestamp tick. `same` then does not trust the segment's identity, `grown` returns it as a tail to sum, and today the read would decode the index and write back again.
- The change: a tail whose bytes are the ones summed and that adds nothing, with no attempt file to apply, leaves the projection current. A read then decodes the state alone, after summing that one segment (about 0.3 ms at 256 KB).

A WRITE-BACK THAT FAILS
- A failed or killed write-back never fails the write. The append is done and fsynced before it starts, `save` returns nothing, and its errors are dropped as a reader's are.
- Killed, the store keeps the projection it had, and the next command extends or replays as today.

ANOTHER PROCESS IN BETWEEN
Process B writes between A's release of the store lock and A's write-back.
- B reads the stored projection plus A's record as a tail, and writes back its own projection, which holds both.
- If A's rename lands after B's, the stored projection names the segment at A's length. The next read extends B's record and writes back.
- Either order answers as replay does. The text file's lock serializes the two saves, as for two readers.

fields.title: A tree in sync.git holding content that does not hash to its name is read as it is, and a sync publishes a tip without that folder
fields.description:
What happens: a loose tree in a machine's sync.git whose file holds well-formed content that does not hash to its name (another tree's, an empty tree's) is read for what it holds. Neither bead's own tree walk through the persistent cat-file (beadroll_git::list_tree_with_subtrees) nor git ls-tree checks an object's hash on reading it. The sync then merges as if the folder that tree stands for were empty, and publishes a tip without it. Nothing reports damage. Already so on main before PR #37; found in #37's independent review (item 6), not fixed there.

Scenario (the reviewer's harness, at fetch.fetched): a publishes x, b publishes "from b". a's sync is held after its fetch brought b's tip; b's folder tree under events/ in a's sync.git is unpacked and its loose file replaced by zlib("tree 0\0"). a's sync answers OK, lists only x, and pushes a tip without b's folder. b's next sync puts the folder back.

A third machine c (checked with a variant of the harness, at 4b6bb55 plus the fix for #37's review):
- c had synced "from b" before a's sync: c's next sync publishes b's folder again, and a gets "from b" on its next sync. Nothing lost.
- c had not: c's sync and a's next sync both list only x, and the remote's tip lacks b's folder until b syncs again. If b's machine is gone by then, "from b" is only in the journal's history (1 commit of 4 holds b's folder): no machine and no current tip holds it.

The fix probably belongs where a tree is read: check that what a tree's object holds hashes to its name before a merge trusts it as empty or short, or have the merge refuse to drop another machine's folder it did not itself remove, and call a mismatch local damage (sync.git made again). It must stay off a successful sync's path, or cost no extra git there.

Harness (the reviewer's, read-only): /tmp/claude-1002/-home-aa-Documents-beadroll/29a68d9b-44c6-4545-9d6d-e6169f123973/scratchpad/rev37/harness/mismatch.py and mismatch_publish.py, with beadsim.py and scenarios.py beside them. The third-machine variant: /tmp/claude-1002/-home-aa--herdr-worktrees-beadroll-prune-during-fetch-is-local-damage/ce521bb8-5d27-4ea9-8a71-34785a7d2b33/scratchpad/h6/third.py. Both are scratch and may be gone; the scenario above is enough to rebuild them as a test in hardening::v8::v8_prune_after_a_fetch's style (fetch.fetched, a rust_only machine, a third Machine).

Priority: P2. The data comes back as soon as any machine that holds the folder syncs, and the trigger, a well-formed object under another object's name, is not what a prune or a torn write leaves (those are missing, empty or corrupt objects, which #37 makes local damage). But it is a silent drop from the published tip, so it should not wait long.

data.text: Review of #37 (BLOCK on docs) answered in cafc68b and bb34370. Code: a failed read of a blob of the fetched tip now asks whether sync.git holds that name as a blob, or as an object whose type git cannot read (Link::unreadable). If so, that is local damage, so a manifest or segment blob with a byte changed or cut short, which git reports only as 'unable to stream', makes sync.git again instead of MANIFEST_MISSING/GIT_ERROR on every sync. The rule is sound: index-pack verified every fetched object and bead wrote its own whole. I used the object's type rather than the tree's mode; fetch refuses mismatched types. A failed rev-list stays damage only in git's words: a malformed tree from the remote fails it too, and fetch without transfer.fsckObjects does not refuse one. The guarantee now promises missing objects, the read blob unreadable, or damage git names. 'Damaged', unqualified, would still be untrue, because a tree whose content does not hash to its name is read as it is (roll-dih8.31, P2). Docs: a lost commit cost one error, and only a lost tree or blob under a present commit is never refetched. The macOS cause is now called likely. The CHANGELOG names the five objects. R1: the reason I gave for the words-only rev-list rule was false; a fetch does refuse a malformed tree, and its connectivity check walks every object it brings. So a rev-list of a present tip that git ends by its own exit is now local damage. That closes the stuck GIT_ERROR 'too-short tree object' for a malformed tree in sync.git, tested for b's folder and the root tree. I found no cause other than damage for such a failure on a whole sync.git: a blob, tree or tag tip walks fine, and fsck-level oddities walk fine. git's own exit on resource exhaustion (malloc failure, too many open files) would also be taken as damage and cost one rebuild, but on Linux an OOM ends git by a signal, and git retries on too many open files, so I kept the rule. Independent review of PR #38 (head 12879c8, base 09bc76b): BLOCK. No wrong answer, output or exit code was found; the block is a cost.

Finding 1 (HIGH): a write's write-back puts that write in the stored projection's frontier, so a merge of another machine's event made before it saw that write is concurrent with the frontier and replays the journal, where roll-lqjj.36's refinement (the maintainer's decision of 2026-10-16) had it extend. fields.description: Link::manifest (crates/beadroll-sync/src/link/read.rs) reads <tip>:manifest.json with git cat-file blob, and when that read fails and Link::lost finds nothing of the fetched tip missing or damaged in sync.git, it returns None: the tip is taken to hold no manifest blob, and the sync answers MANIFEST_MISSING ('has no manifest; refusing to adopt it'), an error about the remote. When the read failed because a signal ended git (beadroll_git::Output::killed, as an OOM killer might do), the remote is not at fault and nothing is known about the tip's tree, so GIT_ERROR (the failed git, 'killed by SIGKILL') would be accurate. Since roll-dih8.30 (PR #37) such a git is correctly never taken as local damage, so this is the only misreport left; the base answered the same. Scenario: the reviewer's harness killed_reads.py (rev37 harness of the second review of #37) runs machine a's syncs with a git wrapper first on PATH that makes bead's long-lived cat-file --batch-command reader exit at once and kills every 'git cat-file blob' with SIGKILL, on a sync.git that is whole, after machine b created an issue. Every sync answers MANIFEST_MISSING with no damaged copies (on 09bc76b and on 9bcd23a); a sync without the wrapper then succeeds. Fix: in Link::manifest, when lost finds nothing and the read was killed, return the read's failure (Output::failed) instead of None; test it as a unit test of the classification, since tests cannot put a wrapper before git.

It parses a meta.json whose published map has N entries shaped as the attempt files' are, then models the map's members built once (one Object, with capacity) and twice (an IndexMap by key bytes holding the text, then the Object, as Members::finish built every object), and parses every line of a history of N events, each segment's and each attempt file's, as the journal reader does.

What it cost on main (4c29f43):
- meta.json of 92,000 files (6.7 MB): 51.6 ms parsed; its 92,006 members built once 7.2 ms, twice 38.2 ms. So the double build is about 31 ms of the 52, three fifths of the parse; scanning and the strings are the rest.

Members is built once, by key as read, while no key holds a lone surrogate (Members::Plain: the Object itself and a flag per member for a value's surrogate, so one a repeated key replaced is still not reported); the first key with a lone surrogate turns it into the old map by key as written (Members::Raw), merged again by key as read at the close, so two keys written apart that read alike merge as before. Investigated whether a JSON library should replace core's parser (the maintainer's question, 2026-10-22), with a benchmark outside the repository (the probe's histories copied, this machine's three real trackers' journals, a meta.json of 92,000 files; fastest of 7 runs, release, default target features and target-cpu=native alike within noise; Threadripper 3970X). Readers: core at main ef0f2ea (after .49), serde_json Value, serde_json into a typed Event struct, simd-json 0.18 OwnedValue, sonic-rs 0.5 Value, jiter 0.17 (owned tree; borrowed tree, shape only; its owned tree converted into core's Value), json 0.12.

Semantics decide before speed. Only core reads a lone surrogate escape (as U+FFFD, reported) and raw lone-surrogate bytes: simd-json turns \ud800 into U+0000 silently, the others refuse. Only core and jiter keep a 30-digit integer exact: serde_json and sonic-rs read it as a float, simd-json refuses it. simd-json, sonic-rs and jiter keep a duplicate key as two members (core: the last value in the first position). serde_json without preserve_order sorts keys. sonic-rs dies with SIGABRT at nesting 100,000 (core refuses past 512; the others refuse at 128 to 1,024). jiter reads 1e400 as infinity though asked for finite numbers (core refuses it), and its recursion limit is 200. Floats agree bit for bit between core and jiter on 12 tricky texts. So serde_json, simd-json, sonic-rs and json 0.12 are out on correctness alone, and jiter would need a wrapper: duplicates collapsed, infinities refused, and core's parser as the fallback for every refusal (lone surrogates, depth 201 to 512, the diagnostics in Python's words).

Speed on 200,000 plain lines (53 MB): core 0.57 s; serde_json Value 0.34; serde_json typed Event 0.26; simd-json 0.43; sonic-rs 0.16; jiter owned 0.22, borrowed shape-only 0.15; jiter owned converted into core's Value 0.37; json 0.12 0.29. 100,000 ownership lines (37 MB): core 0.33, jiter to core 0.21. 50,000 text lines (39 MB): core 0.20, jiter to core 0.13. The real trackers' 3,054 lines (6.3 MB): core 23 ms, jiter to core 13 ms. meta.json of 92,000 files (6.7 MB): core 27 to 31 ms, jiter to core 13 ms, jiter owned 6.5 ms. Core's two pre-passes cost little: the nesting count 31 ms of the 570, and std's UTF-8 validation 9 ms as a floor for check_utf8. A first cut of core's Value built straight from jiter's pull API was no faster than the conversion (0.65 s on plain lines, cause not traced).

Reading: a faithful jiter path would save about 35% of line parsing and half of meta.json, for 18 new crates (ahash, bitvec, lexical-parse-float, num-bigint and their trees), a second parser kept equal to the first (a differential fuzz target), and the fallback. The borrowed-shape figure says a scalar parser without SIMD scans these bytes nearly four times faster than core builds its tree, and jiter's own owned tree that core's scanner and string building take roughly twice what jiter's do; IndexMap building and the pre-passes are the smaller part. Recommendation, the decision being the maintainer's: keep the own parser, and spend this issue on its scanner and strings, with jiter's figures as the target.

Correction to the matrix above: the semantics core keeps (lone surrogate as U+FFFD and reported, integers to 4,300 digits, last-wins duplicates, CPython-worded diagnostics) are Python-port parity pinned by the port ledger and the parser's own fixtures, not external need. bd (Go) never writes a lone surrogate or an integer beyond int64; bead refuses both at write since reviews 5/6; the three real trackers on this machine hold none in 2,950 lines, nor any float. What is immovable: the bytes bead writes (the writer, untouched), every machine reading bead's own lines identically (plain JSON every parser measured reads the same), and import refusing what bead cannot hold (any strict parser). Key order needs no feature: a serde visitor into IndexMap sees document order. So a parser change alters only how hostile or pre-cutover lines are reported, a maintainer decision like U06. The bigger option it opens: deserialize journal lines straight into the event struct with serde instead of a Value tree (serde_json typed 0.26 s against 0.57 for 200,000 lines; sonic-rs likely lower), which the ~35% of a library under the Value tree cannot reach.

Maintainer, 2026-10-22: the Python bead was a proof of concept never used on any project; there is no need for Python parity. The parity-driven semantics listed above are therefore free to change. Measuring typed deserialization (journal line straight into a record struct, no Value tree) with serde_json, sonic-rs and simd-json next.

Typed deserialization measured (journal line straight into a record shaped like journal/event.rs Read+Rest and op.rs Op, fields kept in written order by a serde visitor, no Value tree except actor/where/meta; fastest of 7, release, same runs as core, machine under other load): 200,000 plain lines core 0.56 s, serde_json 0.39-0.41, sonic-rs 0.37, simd-json 0.33; 100,000 ownership lines core 0.31, serde_json 0.14, sonic-rs 0.13, simd-json 0.17; 50,000 text lines core 0.20, serde_json 0.09, sonic-rs 0.09, simd-json 0.11; the real trackers' 3,230 lines core 23 ms, serde_json 10, sonic-rs 8, simd-json 10. Core's figure excludes the extraction into the journal's record that the typed readers already include, so the ratio (1.4x plain, about 2x and more for everything with text) is conservative. The three libraries are within noise of each other on bead's lines; serde_json is the one to take: no SIMD or unsafe, a built-in recursion limit (sonic-rs aborts the process on deep input, simd-json needs a mutable buffer), already a dependency of pancake-studio, and the derive gives the record its types for free. Proposal: reframe this issue as reading journals, attempts and meta.json with serde_json into typed records and retiring the own parser; keep core's writer, since format 1 bytes stay frozen.

fields.title: Read JSON with serde_json under core's Value and retire the own parser
fields.description:
The maintainer's decision of 2026-10-22: the Python bead was a proof of concept never used on any project, so there is no need for Python parity, and the own JSON parser (which existed to pass the port's diff harness against CPython) has no reason left. The comments below hold the investigation: the semantics matrix of six libraries, the speed figures, and the typed-deserialization figures.

This issue is the first of three steps, the smallest change that removes the parser: implement serde::Deserialize for core's json::Value by a visitor (integers into Int, an overflowing integer arrives as a float, objects into the IndexMap where a repeated key keeps its first place and last value), make json::parse a thin wrapper over serde_json::from_slice (pancake-studio calls it and reads the value), delete parse.rs, surrogates.rs (nothing can produce a lone surrogate any more, so nothing is preserved across a whole-file rewrite) and the nesting pre-pass, and let the depth ceiling be serde_json's 128 (events may use 100). The writer stays: format 1 bytes are frozen because real trackers exist. Int stays this round.

Expected from the benchmark: about 1.5x on journal lines (serde_json Value 0.34 s against core's 0.57 for 200,000 plain lines) and meta.json at half its time, with about 850 lines of parser gone.

Children: the typed journal reader (2x and more on text) and the parity leftovers.

data.text:
Implemented on branch feature/roll-lqjj.53-serde-json-under-value: serde_json (float_roundtrip on, no preserve_order or arbitrary_precision) reads into core's Value through a Deserialize visitor; parse.rs, surrogates.rs, the nesting pre-pass and the json fuzz target are gone (1,500 lines out, 430 in). Scope that grew while scoping: receipts are parsed back as JSON (settle_commands) and the --json error envelope is JSON for consumers, and both wrote lone surrogate escapes for bytes that are not UTF-8 (json_ascii_bytes), which serde_json refuses; such a byte is now U+FFFD there. machines --name refuses a non-UTF-8 name (VALIDATION) instead of keeping its bytes as surrogate escapes in aliases.json, and an aliases.json holding one is unreadable: kept, named by the error, naming nobody. Depth ceiling 127 (serde_json's); an integer beyond u64/i64 reads as a float, which replay and the published counts take as a float (the parity fixture's -1e44 count now reads 100000000000000008821361405306422640701865987).

Measured (release, this machine with two QEMU VMs running beside it all afternoon): cargo xtask timing --parse 200000: meta.json of 200,000 files 39 ms (was 67); the probe's synthetic lines 0.69 s (was 0.57), a regression on that input. A/B alternated and pinned to one core: old core 0.55, serde_json's own Value 0.58, new core 0.63-0.67 on those lines (the IndexMap tree with SipHash and a Box per object costs the tenth over serde_json's BTreeMap tree; pre-sizing the map changed nothing, reverted); the three real trackers' 3,230 lines 14 ms (was 24); meta.json of 92,000 files 17 ms (was 27). Caveat: the same serde_json binary read the synthetic lines in 0.34 s this morning on the quieter machine against core's 0.57, and 0.58 against 0.55 now, so serde_json's throughput moved 1.7x with the environment while the old parser's did not; the text figures are bead's real data and held. Acceptance ("measurably lower" on --parse 200000) is met for meta.json and real lines, not for the synthetic lines; the maintainer decides whether that stands. Baseline, clippy, cargo-deny (both workspaces) green locally; fuzz lock updated.

Measured while doing .53: building core's IndexMap tree from serde_json costs about a tenth over serde_json's own BTreeMap tree on 200,000 small lines (0.63-0.67 s against 0.58, pinned, alternated): one SipHash per key and a Box per object. A typed record skips the tree altogether; if the tree stays anywhere (actor, where, an import's extras), an own small hasher for Object (FNV or Fx, no dependency) would take most of the tenth, but Object = IndexMap<String, Value> is a public alias whose new()/with_capacity() exist only for RandomState, so every Object::new() in the workspace and in pancake-studio would become Object::default().
